introduction-the-castle-and-moat-is-dead.core: The castle-and-moat model trusts anything inside the network perimeter. Cloud, remote work, SaaS and lateral movement after a single phished laptop have made that untenable. Zero Trust (NIST SP 800-207) removes implicit trust based on network location: every request, from a user or a workload, is authenticated, authorised against policy and encrypted, using strong identity and device posture, with least privilege and continuous verification. Assume breach.

first_principles.problem: An attacker phishes one VPN user and then reaches every internal database, because 'inside' meant trusted.

analogy.title: An office where every room has its own badge reader
analogy.story: Getting past reception doesn't open the server room; each door checks you again.
analogy.breaks: Badge readers check a card; zero trust also checks context such as device health, time and risk.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Network location no longer grants access.

code.text:
Castle:     src_ip in 10.0.0.0/8            → ALLOW
Zero trust: user=alice@corp (MFA, FIDO2)
            device=managed, disk-encrypted, patched
            resource=payroll-db, action=read
            policy: hr-team AND managed-device → ALLOW (log)

check.q: Does zero trust mean getting rid of firewalls?
check.a: No. Segmentation remains defence in depth, but access decisions are driven by identity and policy, not location.

machine-to-machine-security-standard-tls.core: Standard TLS authenticates only the server: the client checks the server's certificate, but the server learns nothing cryptographic about the client. Mutual TLS (mTLS) adds a client certificate, so both sides prove their identity during the handshake and the connection is encrypted. For service-to-service traffic, mTLS gives strong workload identity without passwords or API keys, as long as certificates are issued, rotated and revoked automatically, usually by a service mesh or SPIFFE.

first_principles.problem: Internal services trust any caller on the network, so a compromised pod can call the payments service freely.
truths: TLS verifies one side by default.

analogy.title: Both people showing ID at a meeting rather than just one
analogy.story: In normal TLS only the shop shows its licence; in mTLS the customer shows ID too.
analogy.breaks: IDs are checked once; mTLS re-proves identity on every new connection.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only the orders service identity can call payments.

code.text:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: { name: default, namespace: payments }
spec: { mtls: { mode: STRICT } }
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-orders, namespace: payments }
spec:
  rules:
    - from: [{ source: { principals: ["cluster.local/ns/orders/sa/orders"] } }]

check.q: What does the server gain from mTLS that it doesn't get from TLS?
check.a: Cryptographic proof of the client's identity, which it can use for authorisation.

the-challenge-who-issues-the-passports.core: mTLS requires every workload to have a certificate, and that raises the bootstrapping question: how does a newly started pod or VM prove who it is to get its first certificate, without a pre-shared secret (secret zero)? The answer is attestation by the platform: the issuer verifies facts it can trust independently, such as Kubernetes service-account tokens, AWS instance identity documents, or TPM quotes, and issues a short-lived identity based on them. SPIFFE standardises the format; SPIRE implements the issuer.

first_principles.problem: Teams copy a shared client certificate into every service so that mTLS 'works', which defeats per-workload identity.

analogy.title: A passport office that issues passports based on birth certificates from the hospital
analogy.story: You don't bring a password; a trusted authority vouches for facts about you.
analogy.breaks: Passports last ten years; workload identities last minutes to hours.

example.title: Bootstrapping flow
flow: Agent attests pod (K8s API: ns, SA)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each pod gets its own identity with no pre-shared secret.

check.q: Why is copying one client cert into every service bad?
check.a: Every service looks identical, so you lose per-service authorisation and a leak compromises all of them.

workload-identity-spiffe-and-spire.core: SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) is a standard for workload identity: a SPIFFE ID URI such as spiffe://prod.example.com/ns/payments/sa/api, carried in an SVID (an X.509 certificate or JWT), delivered via a local Workload API. SPIRE is the reference implementation. A server acts as CA and policy store, and agents on each node attest nodes and workloads (by K8s, AWS, Docker or Unix attributes) and deliver auto-rotating SVIDs. Trust bundles can be federated across clusters and clouds.

first_principles.problem: Services across Kubernetes, VMs and two clouds need one consistent identity system for mTLS and authorisation.
truths: Workloads shouldn't handle key generation themselves.
derivation: Apps fetch SVIDs from the **Workload API**.

analogy.title: An international passport standard
analogy.story: Every country issues passports differently, but the format is the same, so any border can read them.
analogy.breaks: Passports are manually checked; SVIDs are verified automatically on each connection.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each matching pod gets a unique, rotating identity.

code.text:
spire-server entry create \
  -spiffeID spiffe://prod.example.com/ns/payments/sa/api \
  -parentID spiffe://prod.example.com/agent/k8s-node \
  -selector k8s:ns:payments -selector k8s:sa:api -x509SVIDTTL 3600
# the pod's Envoy fetches its SVID over the Workload API socket

check.a: Attributes, such as namespace, service account or image, that a workload must match to receive a given SPIFFE ID.

human-access-the-problem-with-vpns-and-t.core: VPNs put a user's device onto the network, granting broad reach after a single authentication. That's the castle model again: compromised laptops can scan and pivot, credentials are long-lived, and access is coarse. Identity-aware access proxies (HashiCorp Boundary, Teleport, Cloudflare Access, Google IAP) instead broker per-session access to specific targets based on SSO identity, device posture and policy, inject short-lived credentials, never expose the network, and record sessions.

first_principles.problem: A contractor's VPN access, meant for one database, lets their infected laptop scan the whole 10.0.0.0/8 range.
truths: Network access is broader than needed.

analogy.title: A concierge who escorts you to one room versus giving you a master building key
analogy.story: You reach the room you need, the concierge logs the visit, and you never wander the corridors.
analogy.breaks: An escort is a person; proxies enforce this programmatically for thousands of sessions.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One target, short-lived creds, full audit, no network exposure.

code.text:
boundary authenticate oidc            # SSO + MFA
boundary connect postgres -target-id ttcp_orders_db -dbname orders
# Vault-brokered DB creds injected for this session only;
# no network route to the DB from the laptop

check.q: Why don't users need DB passwords with Boundary + Vault?
check.a: Credentials are generated and injected per session by the broker, so users never see or keep them.
